Q: Difference between sh and Bash A:

They're nearly identical, but Bash (executable bash) has more features – sh is (more or less) an older subset of Bash.

sh often means the original Bourne shell, which predates Bash (Bourne again shell), and was created in 1977.

However, in practice, it may be better to think of sh as a highly-cross-compatible shell compliant with the POSIX standard from 1992.

Scripts that start with #!/bin/sh or use the sh shell usually do so for backwards compatibility. Any Unix or Linux OS will have an sh shell. On Ubuntu, sh often invokes Dash and on macOS it's a special POSIX version of Bash. These shells may be preferred for standard-compliant behavior, speed or backwards compatibility.

Bash is newer than the original sh, adds more features, and seeks to be backwards compatible with sh. sh programs will usually run just fine in Bash. Bash is available on nearly all Linux or Unix machines and usually used by default – with the notable exception of macOS defaulting to Z shell (executable zsh) as of Catalina (10.15). FreeBSD, by default, does not come with Bash installed.

Thank you all. I am still getting the hang of the language and proper terms. I am using Oracle DB. Also, yes, I did need to reference the table in the select expression (SELECT tablename.*). Found a work around:
